purpose: Structural benchmark corpus for Oxford-like problem authoring without reproducing source questions.
copyright_policy: Store source references and abstract structural summaries only. Do not copy full problem statements, full transcripts, or solution prose.

evidence_labels.official-sample: University/department publishes the item specifically as a sample interview question.
evidence_labels.actual-used: First-party source says the problem or an adapted version was used in an Oxford interview.
evidence_labels.interview-style-extension: Oxford preparation material explicitly says an item/extension could or has been used to begin an interview.
evidence_labels.subject-adjacent-actual-used: Actual Oxford Maths/CS or CS interview evidence; useful but not treated as pure Maths frequency evidence.
evidence_labels.official-interviewer-used: A first-party Oxford Mathematics resource or Oxford interviewer explicitly says the family was used in Oxford Mathematics interviews.
evidence_labels.official-oxford-academic-used: An Oxford Mathematics tutor/academic explicitly identifies the family as a real/past Oxford admissions interview question; college or departmental material corroborates the role where available.
evidence_labels.official-preparation-example: First-party Oxford admissions preparation material explicitly frames the extension as suitable for starting/continuing an interview, but does not claim it was used.
evidence_labels.official-preparation-borrowed: First-party Oxford interview-preparation material discusses a family while explicitly crediting it to another institution/source; useful for structure but not Oxford-origin provenance.

benchmarks.opening_style: Concrete visual motion with an intuitive prediction before formal modelling.

progression.summary: Predict and/or sketch the locus traced by a marked point during a constrained motion.
Draw several positions and form a hypothesis.
Replace the sketch with variables and a geometric constraint.
Use the invariant geometric relation to characterize the locus.
Move the marked point away from the midpoint and determine how the locus changes.

tutor_interventions: Ask how the candidate could test an initially visual hypothesis.
If stuck, direct attention to the geometric shape formed at every position rather than giving the locus.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Makes abstraction and modelling visible; an intuitive answer can be checked and corrected mathematically.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: physical motion -> geometric constraint -> algebraic locus -> parameterized family
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor commentary explicitly emphasizes abstraction, modelling, testing a hypothesis, and generalising beyond an inaccurate sketch.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No full source wording stored.

benchmarks.opening_style: Low-prerequisite enumeration of the first few small cases.

progression.summary: Draw/count cases for the first few sizes.
Explain systematically why a listed case count has no omissions.
Use additional values to identify a recurrence-like pattern; knowing its conventional name is irrelevant.
Explain structurally why the recurrence occurs.
Change grid dimension and tile shape, then reuse or revise the learned decomposition.

tutor_interventions: Explicitly reassure that an immediate answer is not expected and suggest small cases.
Provide later numerical values to expose a pattern when useful.
Continue giving hints in the modified problem while testing whether earlier ideas were absorbed.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Very low knowledge burden with a high ceiling and repeated opportunities to show learning.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: finite examples -> recurrence -> structural decomposition -> altered combinatorial system
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor explicitly says the knowledge content is no more than GCSE while the internal complexity can test very strong candidates.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No full source wording stored.

source.provenance_note: Oxford states this is adapted from a question James Munro used for Maths interviews.

benchmarks.opening_style: Sketch a simple parameterised function using qualitative behavior before deep calculation.

progression.summary: Describe small/large-input behavior and locate the turning point of a parameterised curve.
Reason qualitatively about composing the function without expanding everything.
Iterate the map and predict the long-run behavior.
Prove a quantitative local bound and interpret the speed of convergence.

tutor_interventions: Prompt with asymptotic behavior at small and large inputs.
Ask for qualitative composition reasoning before algebraic substitution.
Escalate to a quantitative bound only if the interview supports it.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Combines school-level technique with genuine mathematical thinking, iteration, and a very high ceiling.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: graph features -> function composition -> dynamical iteration -> local quantitative estimate
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The official solution explicitly makes the final quantitative proof contingent on how the interview is going.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Only structural description stored; formula omitted from this corpus.

benchmarks.opening_style: Classify feasible small sizes for a geometric tiling construction.

progression.summary: Try small values and draw explicit constructions.
Strengthen an informal impossibility claim by focusing on local/corner structure.
Recognize operations that generate further feasible sizes.
Combine impossibility reasoning and constructions into a broader description.

tutor_interventions: Redirect a weak impossibility argument to a more local geometric feature.
Ask targeted questions about corners/rectangle placement.
Use earlier constructions to prompt a reusable growth rule.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Shows real-time recovery from mistakes and how tutor input can reveal, rather than replace, a candidate's thinking.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: small constructions -> local obstruction -> generative construction -> classification
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Post-interview tutor commentary emphasizes thought process, creativity, pattern spotting, persistence, and use of a newly noticed construction.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No transcript or full statement reproduced.

source.caveat: Use for structural evidence, not pure Mathematics topic-frequency estimates.

benchmarks.opening_style: Constrained selection problem where small cases expose interaction between two rules.

progression.summary: Test small admissible values and try a simple selection strategy.
Pair complementary objects so one global constraint becomes local.
Notice when the forbidden-object condition interacts with the pairing rule.
Change the power/forbidden class and determine what carries over.
If time remains, count the valid selections rather than only decide existence.

tutor_interventions: Suggest small cases early if the candidate does not.
Help isolate the interaction of the two constraints rather than naming a theorem.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Tests whether a candidate can connect two elementary areas without being told the connection.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: examples -> complementary pairing -> hidden interaction -> altered exponent/class
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor explicitly says complete polished solutions are not the point and that small cases may be prompted.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Problem details deliberately abstracted.

source.caveat: Use for structural evidence, not pure Mathematics topic-frequency estimates.

benchmarks.opening_style: Concrete digit manipulation admits an algorithmic trial approach before formalization.

progression.summary: Run a familiar digit-by-digit procedure to generate information.
Notice that a small state determines the next state.
Use finite-state repetition/uniqueness to justify why the procedure eventually cycles or terminates as claimed.
Encode the digit movement as an algebraic equation.
Replace the digit and multiplier with parameters and ask when the construction exists.

tutor_interventions: Encourage starting the mechanical process rather than waiting for a closed form.
Prompt the candidate to identify what information determines the next step.
Accept either procedural or algebraic routes and compare them.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Creates multiple viable representations and lets the candidate develop an algorithm into a proof.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: concrete process -> state machine -> finiteness argument -> algebraic encoding -> parameterized family
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Tutor commentary says the subtle full proof was not expected without help and values the mathematical reasoning about the procedure.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Problem details deliberately abstracted.

source.provenance_note: The author explicitly describes how the underlying item could begin an interview.

benchmarks.opening_style: Begin from an elementary symmetry/area observation in a familiar regular shape.

progression.summary: Identify an area-bisecting line in a symmetric figure.
Ask whether the same centre/bisection relationship holds for other regular polygons.
Make the meaning of 'centre' precise enough for the discussion.
Separate a sufficient-looking symmetry observation from what is actually proved.
Search for other shapes where centre lines bisect area and test converses.

tutor_interventions: Avoid detailed area calculation and focus on symmetry/definition.
Ask whether the observed property is sufficient or merely suggestive.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Turns an easy-looking geometry fact into a proof/definition/generalization discussion.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: familiar symmetry -> generalized claim -> define centre -> test sufficiency/converse
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Official preparation material explicitly frames this as an interview continuation.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No original wording stored.

benchmarks.opening_style: A geometric relation is derived first; its algebraic meaning is then extracted.

progression.summary: Establish a length relation in a simple circle configuration.
Recognize the relation as a general inequality between positive quantities.
Use the geometry to justify the inequality.
Apply it to reciprocal expressions or fixed-perimeter optimization.

tutor_interventions: Keep the geometric interpretation active rather than immediately naming the inequality.
After deriving it, ask for applications in algebra/optimization.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Strong example of learning a tool inside the interview and immediately transferring it.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: geometric identity -> inequality -> algebraic applications -> optimization
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Official material explicitly suggests this kind of extension as an interview continuation.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No source formulas or full problem text stored.

benchmarks.opening_style: Interpret a two-variable equation geometrically instead of solving point-by-point.

progression.summary: Replace an expression in x and y by a radial variable.
Interpret allowed radial values as families of concentric curves.
Reason about spacing as a nonlinear transformation changes.
Change the outer function and predict the new radial graph family.

tutor_interventions: Suggest thinking in terms of radius rather than separate coordinates.
Ask how a nonlinear square-root map changes equal spacings.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Demonstrates that graph sketching can test structure and representation rather than routine plotting.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: two-variable equation -> radius parameter -> family of level sets -> changed outer function
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: Official solutions explicitly describe a related graph as a possible next interview question.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No full equation or answer choices stored.

source.provenance_note: In Oxford Mathematics Plus's 2025 Interview Questions livestream, James Munro says he used this family repeatedly in the preceding admissions cycle. A third-party transcript may be used only to navigate the official recording.

benchmarks.opening_style: A concrete sequential-computation optimisation invites the candidate to try competing operation orders.

progression.summary: Choose an order for a finite sequence of pairwise operations and calculate the resulting total cost.
Compare distinct orders and notice that an apparent optimisation may be invariant.
Rewrite the local cost algebraically so intermediate terms telescope/cancel across the computation tree.
Explain in words why the cancellation makes the total independent of operation order.
Change the local cost rule and test whether order-invariance survives.

tutor_interventions: Clarify the operational process and offload routine arithmetic so multiplication speed is not the target.
Encourage comparing genuinely different orders before asking for a general claim.
After an algebraic proof, ask for a conceptual/verbal account and a changed-cost follow-up.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Begins as an optimisation/search problem, then rewards conjecture, invariant discovery, proof, and explanation across representations.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: operation-order search -> invariant conjecture -> telescoping algebra -> conceptual explanation -> changed local rule
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The official livestream presenter describes the family as useful for seeing a candidate form a hypothesis, prove it, use algebra, and then explain the reason in words.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No full source wording, constants, or derivation stored.

source.provenance_note: James Munro states in the published 2026 Geometry solutions that he has used this investigation as the start of an interview question.

benchmarks.opening_style: A movable point on a familiar curve creates a visual maximisation problem with fixed outer points.

progression.summary: Draw the curve and triangle and identify what changes as the middle point moves.
Treat the fixed chord as a base and reduce area maximisation to maximising perpendicular distance.
Translate the geometric height problem into coordinates/algebra or calculus.
Characterise the optimal position in terms of the fixed endpoints.
Vary the curve or endpoint configuration and ask which geometric idea still applies.

tutor_interventions: If side-length calculations proliferate, redirect attention to fixed-base triangle area.
Allow either geometric or analytic routes and ask the candidate to connect them.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Tests whether the candidate can discard unnecessary calculation and find the representation in which the optimisation becomes simple.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: moving point geometry -> fixed-base height -> analytic representation -> parameterised optimum
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The first-party source explicitly labels the investigation as an interview starter rather than merely a test question extension.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Only the structural fingerprint is retained.

source.provenance_note: Oxford mathematician/interviewer Tom Crawford states that he used the optimisation problem in the 2018 Oxford admissions interviews.

benchmarks.opening_style: A familiar physical design question asks for the most efficient aspect ratio under a fixed-volume constraint.

progression.summary: Express the design objective and fixed resource constraint mathematically.
Eliminate one geometric variable using the constraint.
Optimise the resulting one-variable expression.
Interpret the stationary point and verify that it gives the relevant minimum.
Change the cost model or geometric constraint and predict how the optimal ratio changes.

tutor_interventions: Ask which quantity is fixed and which quantity is being minimised before any differentiation.
If algebra stalls, prompt elimination of one variable rather than supplying the derivative.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Makes modelling choices observable before routine calculus and supports extensions that change assumptions rather than only increase algebra.
oxford_like_features: school calculus used as a tool
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: physical design -> constrained objective -> one-variable reduction -> calculus optimum -> model perturbation
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The source explicitly identifies the family as used in Oxford admissions interviews.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Full original statement and solution omitted.

source.provenance_note: Oxford's Online Maths Club says Tom Crawford presented an interview question he used the previous year; Crawford separately states the rectangle-assembly family was used in the 2020 and 2021 Oxford interview cycles.

benchmarks.opening_style: Classify which counts of congruent fixed-aspect rectangles can assemble into a square.

progression.summary: Try small counts and draw explicit assemblies or identify impossible cases.
Discover constructions that combine or scale known feasible cases.
Explain why exceptional small counts fail rather than relying on unsuccessful drawing.
Use the constructions and obstructions to cover a broad class of counts.
Ask how the classification changes with a different rectangle aspect ratio.

tutor_interventions: Use failed small cases to ask what geometric obstruction is actually being encountered.
Prompt the candidate to reuse a successful tiling as a building block for larger cases.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Combines experimentation, geometric construction, impossibility reasoning, and a high-ceiling classification problem.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: small assemblies -> reusable construction -> exceptional obstructions -> global classification -> aspect-ratio variant
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The family is independently described by an Oxford Maths outreach page and its interviewing tutor as actual admissions-interview material.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No source diagrams or exact classification answer stored.

source.provenance_note: Tom Crawford's University of Oxford-produced video says the exact question was used in his 2018 Oxford Maths interviews; St John's College links these videos as remote-interview-style resources.

assumed_prerequisites: surface/volume of revolution formulas may be supplied
benchmarks.opening_style: A familiar improper integral/solid-of-revolution calculation develops into a counterintuitive comparison between volume and surface area.

progression.summary: Set up and evaluate a volume-of-revolution quantity for a decaying curve.
Set up the corresponding surface-area quantity and compare convergence behavior.
Reconcile the finite/infinite contrast and articulate why intuition initially misleads.
Vary the decay rate and classify when volume and surface area converge.

tutor_interventions: Supply or derive an unfamiliar surface-area element if that formula is outside the candidate's school background.
Ask the candidate to predict convergence before completing every integral.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Uses familiar calculus as an entry point to unfamiliar analysis and invites tutors to teach a needed formula during the interview.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: standard integral -> parallel geometric quantity -> convergence contrast -> parameter classification
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The source identifies this as an exact real Oxford admissions interview question.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No integral formulas or worked solution text copied into the corpus.

source.provenance_note: Tom Crawford describes it as a real Oxford admissions interview question; St John's College lists the video among its interview resources.

assumed_prerequisites: harmonic-series divergence and/or comparison facts may be introduced
benchmarks.opening_style: Start from familiar prime factorisation and finite products/sums before asking about a global property of prime reciprocals.

progression.summary: Relate finite combinations of primes to integers using unique factorisation.
Encode that relationship through a product/sum identity or bound.
Connect the finite structure to a known divergent series and derive the required conclusion.
Discuss which ingredients are essential and what analogous prime-weighted series might do.

tutor_interventions: Introduce a relevant standard series fact if the candidate has not met it.
Prompt expansion of a finite product or comparison with all positive integers rather than naming the final theorem.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Shows how tutors can supply a theorem/fact and assess whether the candidate can combine it with elementary number theory.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: prime factorisation -> finite analytic encoding -> comparison/divergence argument -> weighted-series extension
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The public resource describes this as real Oxford interview material and as the second part of an interview sequence.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: The theorem target and proof are not reproduced verbatim.

source.provenance_note: Oxford Online Maths Club explicitly describes the livestream problem as an Oxford maths interview question and discusses its higher-dimensional spline continuation.

benchmarks.opening_style: Endpoint value/derivative conditions are given and the candidate must construct a cubic satisfying them.

progression.summary: Write a general cubic with unknown coefficients and translate endpoint conditions into equations.
Solve the coefficient system and check all imposed conditions.
Join multiple cubics while matching value, slope, and possibly second derivative.
Recognise the construction as a route toward piecewise polynomial/spline ideas, with unfamiliar terminology introduced after the elementary work.

tutor_interventions: If the full system feels large, isolate one cubic/endpoint at a time.
Introduce the vocabulary of piecewise polynomials or splines only after the candidate has constructed the elementary case.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Starts with school algebra/calculus and naturally teaches a university-level idea without requiring prior knowledge of it.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: conditions -> coefficient system -> constructed function -> smooth piecewise joining -> spline concept
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The official page contrasts the manageable interview version with a harder multi-cubic continuation and notes that the interview version had four parameters.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: No full endpoint system from the original interview problem is stored.

benchmarks.opening_style: Begin from two familiar polynomial inequalities and a truth-table-like interval analysis.

progression.summary: Solve two polynomial sign conditions and identify where both hold.
Construct one polynomial whose sign encodes logical AND of the original conditions.
Change the logical target to exclusive-or/exactly-one.
Ask when such sign encodings work for arbitrary pairs and identify failure modes.

tutor_interventions: Use an interval sign table if the candidate is losing track of cases.
Ask what multiplication does to signs before proposing a general construction.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Turns routine inequalities into an unfamiliar algebra/logic representation problem with clear counterexample opportunities.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: sign intervals -> logical condition -> polynomial encoding -> arbitrary-pair failure analysis
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The current official solutions explicitly say this is how the author might continue the test item as an interview question.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Original polynomials and answer options omitted.

benchmarks.opening_style: A deterministic sequence property is first tested with deliberately chosen examples/counterexamples.

progression.summary: Construct examples to test universal-looking claims about an arithmetic-sequence property.
Derive an algebraic condition for when the property occurs.
Fix one sequence parameter and choose another uniformly from a finite range.
Convert the structural divisibility condition into a probability/counting question.

tutor_interventions: Prompt deliberate backwards construction of a counterexample rather than random guessing.
After deriving the structural condition, ask how often it holds under a simple finite random model.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Connects proof/counterexample work to modelling and probability without requiring advanced probabilistic machinery.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: universal claim -> constructed counterexample -> divisibility condition -> finite random model
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The first-party solution explicitly proposes the probability continuation if used as an interview starter.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: The source's named property and constants are not copied.

benchmarks.opening_style: Work with symmetric expressions in roots without explicitly solving for the roots.

progression.summary: Extract sums/products of roots and evaluate derived symmetric expressions.
Build a related polynomial whose roots are transformed versions of the original roots.
Combine related polynomials and predict the result without brute-force expansion.
If needed, introduce root-coefficient/Vieta language during the interview and ask the candidate to use it.

tutor_interventions: Discourage explicit root solving when symmetric information is enough.
Teach the root-coefficient relationship if it is unfamiliar, then assess whether the candidate can exploit it.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Directly models Oxford's stated format of introducing a new mathematical fact and asking the candidate to draw consequences.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: root data -> symmetric expressions -> transformed-root polynomial -> structural product -> introduced theorem
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The official solution explicitly notes the prerequisite risk and says the relevant formula could be taught during the interview.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Constants and explicit factors from the source are omitted.

benchmarks.opening_style: Estimate intersections between a bounded oscillatory graph and a monotone comparison graph.

progression.summary: Sketch/compare two curves and locate intervals containing crossings.
Check that apparent crossings are not missed or spuriously added by the sketch.
Replace the monotone comparison function with a decaying reciprocal term.
Explain why infinitely many roots now occur and estimate their locations asymptotically/locally.

tutor_interventions: Ask for sign/lead checks at selected landmarks rather than accepting a rough sketch as proof.
For the infinite-root extension, ask where oscillatory peaks occur before requesting approximations.
benchmarks.pedagogical_value: Starts with visual graph reasoning and deepens into rigorous existence/counting and asymptotic approximation.
benchmarks.abstraction_pattern: graph intersections -> interval checks -> changed comparison function -> infinite sequence of roots -> approximation
benchmarks.assessment_commentary: The official solution explicitly gives the reciprocal-function problem as the next interview question.
benchmarks.source_reproduction: Exact coefficients and intervals omitted.

corpus_scope_note: Deep benchmark corpus: selected examples with enough authoritative evidence for structural annotation. It is intentionally non-exhaustive and must never be treated as a whitelist of all Oxford questions.
